summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 and IPv6 Neighbour Discovery so that movement within a local area can be handled locally. A Mobility Anchor Point reduces signalling to the home agent and correspondent nodes and can make handovers faster. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4140.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves to a new part of a network, Mobile IPv6 normally tells its home agent and every contact about it. This RFC puts a router in the visited network that acts as a local home agent, so only that router has to be told about most movements. The device keeps the same address for the whole region, which also hides its exact location.

subtitle: Adds a local anchor router so a device moving inside one network does not have to update distant peers every time.

tldr.problem: In Mobile IPv6, a device sends a binding update to its home agent every time it moves, and route optimisation adds about 1.5 round-trip times of signalling to each correspondent node. The result is delay at handover and a lot of signalling on the wireless link.
tldr.mechanism: A Mobility Anchor Point sits in the visited network and acts as a local home agent. The device registers one regional care-of address with it, and later movements inside the same domain are handled locally by the anchor instead of by the home agent and the correspondent nodes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5380 is a Proposed Standard from October 2008 that obsoletes RFC 4140. It removes dynamic MAP discovery, switches the security section to IKEv2, and states that HMIPv6 can be used without a permanent home agent. Its own appendix records that no deployment was publicly known at the time of writing.

facts.label: MAP failure probe example
facts.value: Every 10 seconds, then every 5 for 15 seconds

today: RFC 5380 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It obsoletes RFC 4140, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its own appendix records that RFC 4140 was implemented and interoperability tested by at least two organisations, but that at the time of writing there was no publicly known deployment of this specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6, RFC 3775, lets nodes move within the Internet topology while keeping reachability and ongoing connections between mobile and correspondent nodes. To do this, a mobile node sends binding updates to its home agent every time it moves. The node may send data packets through the home agent immediately after the binding update, but the home agent cannot route traffic back until the update arrives, which costs at least half a round-trip delay, and more if the node waits for a binding acknowledgement. Round-trip times can be long when the node and its home agent are in different parts of the world.

Route optimisation adds more delay. Authenticating binding updates takes about 1.5 round-trip times between the node and each correspondent node in the best case, with no packet loss, and the RFCs that reduce that figure are cited. The signalling exchanges needed to update a location will always cause some disruption to active connections, and some packets will be lost. On a wireless link, fewer messages over the air is also a direct saving.

The RFC therefore introduces a new Mobile IPv6 node, the Mobility Anchor Point (MAP), which can be located at any level in a hierarchical network of routers, including the Access Router. The MAP limits the amount of Mobile IPv6 signalling outside the local domain. The mobile node sends binding updates to the local MAP rather than to the home agent and the correspondent nodes, and only one binding update needs to be transmitted before traffic from the home agent and all correspondent nodes is re-routed, regardless of how many correspondent nodes the node is talking to. A MAP is essentially a local home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving a device normally means telling everyone where it went. This RFC adds a router nearby that keeps track of the device instead, so the far-away home agent and the contacts only need to hear about the device once, not on every move.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The Access Router (AR) is the mobile node's default router. It aggregates the outbound traffic of mobile nodes. A Mobility Anchor Point is a router located in a network visited by the mobile node, used by the node as a local home agent. One or more MAPs can exist within a visited network.

A Regional Care-of Address (RCoA) is an address allocated by the MAP to the mobile node. The on-link care-of address (LCoA) is the address configured on the mobile node's interface from the prefix advertised by its default router; in RFC 3775 this is simply called the care-of address, and this document uses LCoA to distinguish it from the RCoA.

An HMIPv6-aware mobile node is a node that can receive and process the MAP option received from its default router, and that can send local binding updates, which are binding updates with the M flag set. A local binding update is the message the node sends to the MAP to establish a binding between the RCoA and the LCoA.
sections.plainLanguage: Two addresses matter here. The LCoA is the address the device uses on the link it is attached to, and it changes every time the device changes subnet. The RCoA is an address from the anchor's subnet that stays the same while the device stays in that region.

sections.title: Overview of HMIPv6
sections.content:
The scheme adds the MAP function and minor extensions to the mobile node's operation. The correspondent node and home agent operations are not affected at all. Like Mobile IPv6, the solution is independent of the underlying access technology, so mobility within or between different types of access network is allowed.

A mobile node entering a MAP domain receives Router Advertisements containing information about one or more local MAPs. The node binds its current location, the on-link care-of address, with an address on the MAP's subnet. Acting as a local home agent, the MAP receives all packets on behalf of the mobile node it serves, and encapsulates and forwards them directly to the node's current address. If the node changes address inside the same MAP domain, it only needs to register the new address with the MAP. The Regional CoA therefore needs to be registered with correspondent nodes and the home agent only once, and it does not change as long as the node stays inside a MAP domain. The node's movement is invisible to the correspondent nodes it talks to.

The boundaries of a MAP domain are set by the Access Routers that advertise the MAP information to the attached mobile nodes. An HMIPv6-aware node with a Mobile IPv6 implementation SHOULD choose to use the MAP when it discovers that capability in a visited network, but it may prefer the standard Mobile IPv6 behaviour, for instance when the home agent is located near the visited network. The MAP is not tied to a permanent home agent: a mobile node need not have a permanent home address or home agent to be HMIPv6-aware, and a MAP may be used by a node in a nomadic manner to achieve mobility management within a local domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The anchor router works like a home agent for the devices it serves. A device tells it where it is, and it forwards the device's traffic. Because the device keeps the same regional address while it moves around the region, nobody else has to be told.

sections.title: The MAP Option and the M Flag
sections.content:
Two pieces of wire format are added. The first is a new flag in the binding update of RFC 3775, the M flag, which indicates MAP registration. When a mobile node registers with a MAP, the M and A flags MUST be set to distinguish this registration from a binding update sent to the home agent or a correspondent node.

The second is a new option for Router Advertisements, the MAP option, which is an IPv6 Neighbour Discovery option with the value 23. Its Length field is an 8-bit unsigned integer and MUST be set to 3. The Dist field is a 4-bit unsigned integer giving the distance between the MAP and the receiver of the advertisement, measured in hops and starting from 1 if the MAP is on the same link as the mobile node; a distance value of zero MUST NOT be used. The Pref field is a 4-bit unsigned integer used as an indicator of operator preference, where the decimal value 15 indicates the highest preference, and the node SHOULD inspect it as a tie-breaker between MAPs with equal Dist values. The R flag, when set to 1, indicates that the mobile node is allocated the RCoA by the MAP based on Section 9 of RFC 4877. The Valid Lifetime field is the minimum value, in seconds, of both the valid lifetime of the prefix used to form the MAP's address and that used to form the RCoA, so it says how long the MAP's address and the RCoA remain valid. The Global Address field holds one of the MAP's global addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The Router Advertisement carries one extra option that names the anchor router and says how far away it is and how much the operator prefers it. The binding update carries one extra flag that says this registration is for the local anchor rather than for the home agent.

sections.title: Protocol Operation
sections.content:
In HMIPv6 the mobile node has two addresses: an RCoA on the MAP's link and an on-link care-of address. The RCoA is formed statelessly by combining the node's interface identifier with the subnet prefix received in the MAP option.

When a node moves into a new MAP domain, it configures both addresses and, after acquiring an RCoA using RFC 4877, sends a local binding update to the MAP with the A and M flags set. The local binding update is a binding update of RFC 3775 that carries the RCoA in the Home Address option and needs no alternate care-of address option; the LCoA is the source address of the message. The MAP, acting as a home agent, returns a binding acknowledgement that either identifies the binding as successful or carries the appropriate fault code. No new error codes are needed, and the node MUST silently ignore binding acknowledgements that do not contain a routing header type 2 holding the RCoA.

After a successful registration a bi-directional tunnel between the node and the MAP is established. Packets the node sends are tunnelled to the MAP, with the LCoA in the source field of the outer header and the MAP's address in the destination field, and with the RCoA in the source field of the inner header and the peer's address in the destination field. Packets addressed to the RCoA are intercepted by the MAP and tunnelled to the LCoA.

The node then registers its new RCoA with its home agent by sending a binding update that specifies the binding between the RCoA and the home address, as in Mobile IPv6, and may send a similar update to its current correspondent nodes. It SHOULD wait for the binding acknowledgement from the MAP before registering with other nodes, and the binding lifetime used with the home agent and correspondent nodes MUST NOT be larger than the lifetime of the binding with the MAP.

When the node moves within the same MAP domain, it registers only its new LCoA with the MAP, and the RCoA stays the same. To speed up a handover between MAPs, the node SHOULD send a local binding update to its previous MAP specifying the new LCoA, so that packets still in transit are forwarded to the new address. The MAP has no knowledge of the node's home address, and it may be configured with the list of valid on-link prefixes that nodes may use; a binding update with an LCoA outside that list could be rejected with the existing error code 129, administratively prohibited. HMIPv6 is completely transparent to the home agent and to correspondent nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The device registers with the anchor router by sending it one message that carries both addresses, and the anchor answers with an acknowledgement. Only then does the device tell its home agent and its contacts the new regional address. Moves inside the same region need no message to anybody except the anchor.

sections.title: MAP Discovery and Selection
sections.content:
The RFC requires network administrators to configure the MAP option information in the Access Routers by hand; future mechanisms may allow MAPs to be discovered dynamically, but dynamic MAP discovery was removed from this specification because its scalability was seen as inappropriate for large deployments and prone to loops.

When an HMIPv6-aware node receives a Router Advertisement it looks for the MAP option, and one or more options may be found for different MAP addresses. The node SHOULD register with the MAP having the highest preference value. A MAP with a preference value of zero SHOULD NOT be used for new local binding updates, though the node can refresh existing bindings but not create new ones. A MAP option with a valid lifetime of zero means the MAP MUST NOT be selected: a valid lifetime of zero indicates a MAP failure, so the node MUST choose another MAP and create new bindings, and any existing bindings with that MAP can be assumed lost. If no other MAP is available, the node MUST NOT attempt to use HMIPv6.

The node MUST store the options it receives, because they are compared with later options as part of movement detection. If the R flag is set, the node places its RCoA in place of the home address in the binding update, which causes the RCoA to be bound to the LCoA in the MAP's binding cache.

On selection, the RFC describes an Eager-Lazy approach: the node is eager to perform new bindings and lazy in releasing existing ones. It registers with any new MAP advertised by the Access Router, and does not release existing bindings until it stops receiving the MAP option, receives it with a lifetime of zero, or its binding lifetime expires. This gives a fallback when a MAP router fails, because it shortens the time before the node can tell its correspondent nodes and home agent about a new care-of address.

Where several MAPs are available in one domain, there are no benefits in selecting more than one and forcing packets down a hierarchy of MAPs, since that adds forwarding delays and removes the robustness of IP routing between the highest MAP and the node, so it is prohibited. More than one MAP above the Access Router can still be used for redundancy and as an optimisation, with the node using each MAP independently for a particular set of correspondent nodes. The default selection algorithm parses all MAP options, arranges the MAPs in descending order starting with the furthest one, selects the first, and moves to the next if the preference value or the valid lifetime is zero, repeating until a MAP with non-zero preference and non-zero valid lifetime is found. A mobile node may also register with more than one MAP at the same time, or use both the RCoA and the LCoA as care-of addresses with different correspondent nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The anchor router's details come from the Router Advertisement, and the administrator puts them there. When several anchors are on offer, the device takes the most distant one that the operator prefers and that is still working, so that it does not have to re-register too often.

sections.title: Failure, Recovery and Tunnelling Limits
sections.content:
A MAP, like a home agent, is a single point of failure. If it fails, its binding cache content is lost and communication between the mobile node and its correspondent nodes stops. This can be avoided by using more than one MAP on the same link and a context transfer protocol between them, but MAP redundancy is outside the scope of this document.

Where such protocols are not supported, the node detects the failure when it receives a Router Advertisement containing a MAP option with a lifetime of zero. It then starts MAP discovery and tries to register with another MAP, and if its RCoA has changed it must also inform the correspondent nodes and the home agent. Where a protocol transfers binding cache entries between MAPs for redundancy, a new MAP may be able to offer the same RCoA, for example when both MAPs advertise the same prefix, which saves the node from updating the correspondent nodes and the home agent.

An Access Router can be triggered to advertise a MAP option with a lifetime of zero by manual intervention or in a dynamic manner. One dynamic method is to probe the MAP regularly, for example every 10 seconds; if no response arrives, the Access Router may probe more aggressively for a short period, for example once every 5 seconds for 15 seconds, and if there is still no reply it may send a MAP option with a valid lifetime of zero. The exact probing mechanism is out of scope, and this method may not detect a failure that happens between probes. The specification does not mandate a recovery mechanism, but any mechanism between the MAP and an Access Router SHOULD be secure enough to allow message authentication, integrity protection and protection against replay attacks.

Tunnelling has a cost. The node tunnels its outgoing traffic to the MAP and the MAP tunnels inbound packets to the node, so a node whose home agent is elsewhere on the Internet results in double encapsulation of both inbound and outbound packets. Mobile nodes MUST therefore take the encapsulation between the node and the MAP into account when calculating the MTU available to upper layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The anchor router is a single point of failure, so the network needs a way to notice when it stops working and point the device at another one. Because traffic is wrapped twice, the packet budget available to applications is smaller than on a plain link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security relationship between the mobile node and the MAP must be strong. It MUST involve mutual authentication, integrity protection and protection against replay attacks. Confidentiality may be needed for payload traffic, for example when the node is unwilling to reveal any traffic to the access network beyond what is needed to attach and to talk to the MAP; it is not required for binding updates to the MAP. Without these protections, a malicious node could impersonate another one or impersonate a MAP, which would disrupt the node's communication with every correspondent node that knows its RCoA.

Initial authorisation to use the MAP's forwarding service MAY be needed. Authorising a node can be based on its identity exchanged during security association negotiation, and the authorisation may be granted on the identity of the node or on the identity of a certificate authority the MAP trusts. This level of authorisation is independent of authorising the use of a particular RCoA, and in this specification authentication and authorisation are effectively the same thing: all the MAP needs in order to allocate an RCoA is to authenticate the node and verify that it belongs to a trusted group. Trusted third-party certificates are not required, and some deployments would be satisfied with self-signed certificates for either side.

IKEv2 MUST be supported by the mobile node and the MAP, and IKEv2 allows EAP to bootstrap the security association. A MAP MAY support EAP over IKEv2, in which case the EAP method runs between the node and a AAA server and the resulting keying material bootstraps IKEv2 between the MAP and the node.

Because the MAP has no prior knowledge of the node's identity or home address, the security association can be established with any key establishment protocol such as IKEv2, and a return routability test is not necessary. The MAP sets the security association for the RCoA rather than the LCoA, achieved by using the RCoA as the identity in the IKE CHILD_SA negotiation, which is identical to using the home address when negotiating with the home agent. The IPsec Peer Authorization Database entries and configuration payloads of RFC 4877 for allocating dynamic home addresses SHOULD be used to allocate the RCoA. Binding updates between the MAP and the node MUST be protected with either the Authentication Header or the Encapsulating Security Payload in transport mode, and when ESP is used a non-null authentication algorithm MUST be used.

The return routability test of RFC 3775 is not affected, but implementers must be careful about the source address of the HoTI and CoTI messages: it SHOULD be the home address unless the node is using the RCoA for route optimisation. The packet carrying the HoTI message is encapsulated twice, with the RCoA in the inner header and the LCoA in the outer header. The security relationship with the home agent is not impacted by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The link between the device and the anchor router has to be protected in both directions, so that nobody else can register the device's regional address and steal its traffic. The RFC requires IKEv2 for that, and allows the account infrastructure to be used to set it up.

fields.desc: One of the MAP's global addresses.
